description_under_test: Audit a schema, migration, or PR diff against Taleemabad's 27 Data Standards (D1-D27, tiered NON-NEGOTIABLE/ESSENTIAL/ADVANCED/SPECIALIZED, across Lesson Plans, Digital Coach, Teacher Training, Exam Generator, User Mgmt, Data & Analytics). Use when reviewing a schema change, writing a migration, designing a new table, or asked "does this meet our data standards" / "is this PII-safe" / "what does D6 require" / "give me a compliance audit report".
source: Stage-1 enforcement-core build (2026-08-17): shared detector + validator + narrow Claude PreToolUse gate. Trigger cases follow the pack's established evals.json convention (see curriculum-baked-lesson-plans/evals/evals.json); correctness/hygiene/determinism cases are this skill's own addition since audit correctness is the higher-risk failure mode here (a wrong report is worse than a wrong trigger).
method: Trigger cases: run each query in a fresh session 3x; a should_trigger case passes above a 0.5 trigger rate, a should_not case passes below it. Correctness/hygiene/determinism cases: run the named script/fixture combination and check the assertion — these are deterministic (no model variance), so a single run either passes or fails.

cases.query: does this migration meet our data standards?
audit this schema for compliance issues
is this table PII-safe?
what does D6 require?
give me a compliance audit report for this PR
I'm about to add a new column to the users table, check it against our standards

correctness_cases.fixture: evals/fixtures/clean_migration.sql
correctness_cases.command: python3 scripts/validate_schema.py --mode full --path <fixture-dir>
correctness_cases.why_it_matters: A compliant migration (UUID PKs, TIMESTAMPTZ, FK present, PII column with a classification comment) must produce ZERO findings — a false positive here is exactly what gets a gate disabled by an annoyed team. This case exists because an earlier build of validate_schema.py's column-comment parser DID false-positive on this exact fixture (misattributed a PII classification comment to the wrong column) before the bug was caught and fixed.

correctness_cases.fixture: evals/fixtures/violating_migration.sql
correctness_cases.command: python3 scripts/validate_schema.py --mode full --path <fixture-dir>
correctness_cases.why_it_matters: A migration with a SERIAL (not UUID) PK, an unclassified phone column, a bare TIMESTAMP, a dangling FK-shaped column, and no migration-tool marker must produce exactly these 5 confirmed findings with exact location evidence.

correctness_cases.fixture: evals/fixtures/classified_pii_migration.sql
correctness_cases.command: python3 scripts/validate_schema.py --mode full --path <fixture-dir>
correctness_cases.why_it_matters: Two consecutive PII-pattern columns (cnic, email), each with its own classification comment, one of which has a comma INSIDE its comment's prose — this is the specific edge case that broke the column parser during development. Must stay green on every future change to validate_schema.py.

correctness_cases.fixture: evals/fixtures/destructive_migration.sql
correctness_cases.command: python3 scripts/validate_schema.py --mode full --path <fixture-dir>
correctness_cases.why_it_matters: A DROP TABLE and a DROP COLUMN with no rollback plan or reviewed marker must both block — per enforcement-policy.md, a destructive migration without safety metadata is a deterministic blocking finding, not advisory.

correctness_cases.fixture: evals/fixtures/destructive_migration_reviewed.sql
correctness_cases.command: python3 scripts/validate_schema.py --mode full --path <fixture-dir>
correctness_cases.why_it_matters: The same class of destructive statement (DROP TABLE), but with a `-- destructive: reviewed` marker and rationale, must pass — the safety-metadata escape hatch documented in enforcement-policy.md must actually work, not just be documented.

correctness_cases.fixture: (empty directory, or any non-.sql file)
correctness_cases.command: python3 scripts/validate_schema.py --mode full --path <empty-dir>
correctness_cases.why_it_matters: Exit code 3 ("no schema-related change detected") must be distinguishable from exit 0 ("checked, and it passed") — an enforcement layer that treats these the same would silently skip real audits whenever the detector finds nothing to check, without anyone noticing the check never ran.

correctness_cases.fixture: (a hand-written malformed JSON report file)
correctness_cases.command: python3 scripts/validate_schema.py --mode validate-report <malformed.json>
correctness_cases.why_it_matters: A malformed report (or, by extension, a validator that can't run at all) must produce exit 2, distinct from both a pass (0) and a confirmed failure (1) — per enforcement-policy.md, an enforcement layer must never treat 'the check itself broke' the same as 'the check ran and found nothing.'

correctness_cases.fixture: evals/fixtures/violating_migration.sql
correctness_cases.command: python3 scripts/validate_schema.py --mode full --path <fixture-dir> (run 3x)
correctness_cases.expect: identical JSON output (findings, order, evidence text) on all 3 runs
correctness_cases.why_it_matters: A static analyzer that reorders findings or varies its output run-to-run makes 'did this get fixed' impossible to answer by diffing two audit runs — every check in validate_schema.py is pure regex/string parsing over the same input text, so this should hold trivially, but it's asserted explicitly rather than assumed.

correctness_cases.fixture: evals/fixtures/violating_migration.sql, staged in a scratch git repo
correctness_cases.command: echo '{"tool_name":"Bash","tool_input":{"command":"git commit -m x"}}' | bash hooks/schema-change-gate.sh
correctness_cases.why_it_matters: The PreToolUse hook itself (not just the validator it calls) must actually block a git commit when the staged change has a confirmed violation — end-to-end, not just at the validator layer. This is the exact case that exposed a real bug during development: INPUT_JSON was read by a Python subprocess before being exported to its environment, so the hook silently no-op'd (exit 0) on every input until the export-ordering was fixed.

correctness_cases.fixture: evals/fixtures/clean_migration.sql, staged in a scratch git repo
correctness_cases.command: echo '{"tool_name":"Bash","tool_input":{"command":"git commit -m x"}}' | bash hooks/schema-change-gate.sh
correctness_cases.why_it_matters: The gate must not block a compliant change — a gate that blocks everything is as useless as one that blocks nothing, and gets disabled just as fast.

correctness_cases.fixture: n/a
correctness_cases.command: echo '{"tool_name":"Bash","tool_input":{"command":"ls -la"}}' | bash hooks/schema-change-gate.sh
correctness_cases.why_it_matters: Per Anthropic hook-hygiene guidance, a hook must exit fast and cheap on every irrelevant call rather than running the validator before every single Bash command.

correctness_cases.fixture: n/a
correctness_cases.command: echo '{"tool_name":"Bash","tool_input":{"command":"echo about to git commit soon"}}' | bash hooks/schema-change-gate.sh
correctness_cases.why_it_matters: The string "git commit" appearing inside an echo/prose command must not trip the gate — only an actual git-commit invocation should. A substring match here would false-trigger constantly.

correctness_cases.fixture: n/a
correctness_cases.command: echo '{not json' | bash hooks/schema-change-gate.sh
correctness_cases.why_it_matters: A hook that crashes or hangs on malformed stdin would break every subsequent tool call in the session — malformed input must fail safe (exit 0, do nothing) per Anthropic hook-security guidance, never fail closed by accident.

correctness_cases.fixture: evals/fixtures/violating_migration.sql, staged, CLAUDE_DATA_STANDARDS_GATE_OFF=1 exported (no TALEEMABAD_DATA_STANDARDS_BYPASS)
correctness_cases.command: export CLAUDE_DATA_STANDARDS_GATE_OFF=1; echo '{...git commit...}' | bash hooks/schema-change-gate.sh
correctness_cases.why_it_matters: REVISED 2026-08-19: this case originally asserted expect_exit=0 (the old boolean bypass worked). As of the gate-hook rewrite, CLAUDE_DATA_STANDARDS_GATE_OFF=1 no longer bypasses anything at all -- a boolean escape hatch with zero accountability was replaced by a reason-carrying variable that's actually validated and recorded. This case now asserts the OPPOSITE of what it originally did, on purpose: the commit must still be BLOCKED, and a NOTICE about the retired variable should appear on stderr.

correctness_cases.fixture: evals/fixtures/violating_migration.sql, in a scratch git repo with install_repo_hooks.py run against it
correctness_cases.command: python3 scripts/install_repo_hooks.py --repo <scratch-repo>; then a REAL `git commit` (not a simulated hook invocation) inside that repo with the violating fixture staged
correctness_cases.expect: git commit fails (non-zero exit), the validator's JSON findings print to stderr, and `git commit --no-verify` on the same staged state succeeds
correctness_cases.why_it_matters: This is the strongest verification available for the local hook: not simulating stdin against the hook script directly (that only proves the script's own logic), but actually letting git invoke its own installed pre-commit hook mechanism end to end, on a real commit attempt.

correctness_cases.fixture: evals/fixtures/clean_migration.sql, in a scratch git repo with hooks installed
correctness_cases.command: a real `git commit` with the clean fixture staged, no --no-verify
correctness_cases.expect: commit succeeds normally, exit 0
correctness_cases.why_it_matters: A hook that blocks everything is as useless as one that blocks nothing — must confirm the positive case, not just the block case.

correctness_cases.fixture: a scratch repo with a hand-written, unrelated pre-commit hook already present
correctness_cases.command: python3 scripts/install_repo_hooks.py --repo <scratch-repo>
correctness_cases.expect: pre-commit reported as SKIPPED, the original hook file's content is byte-identical before and after, pre-push (no conflict) still installs normally
correctness_cases.why_it_matters: Per the brief: 'do not overwrite existing hooks.' Silently clobbering a developer's own pre-commit hook (which might do anything — run tests, lint, sign commits) would be a destructive, unannounced side effect. This must be actively defended, not just assumed safe.

correctness_cases.fixture: a scratch repo with one installed (ours) pre-push hook and one pre-existing (not ours) pre-commit hook
correctness_cases.command: python3 scripts/install_repo_hooks.py --repo <scratch-repo> --uninstall
correctness_cases.expect: pre-push removed, pre-commit reported 'skipped (not ours)' and its content untouched
correctness_cases.why_it_matters: An uninstall that removes ANY file named pre-commit/pre-push (rather than only ones this script wrote) would destroy a developer's unrelated hook on --uninstall — the marker-based ownership check must be honored on removal, not just on install.

correctness_cases.fixture: reference/ci-workflow-template.yml
correctness_cases.command: python3 -c "import yaml; yaml.safe_load(open('reference/ci-workflow-template.yml', encoding='utf-8'))"
correctness_cases.expect: parses without error, job name 'data-standards' present
correctness_cases.why_it_matters: A syntactically broken CI template would fail silently (or confusingly) the first time a team tries to adopt it — this is the one thing about the template verifiable without a real GitHub Actions runner, so it's checked. NOTE: open() must specify encoding='utf-8' explicitly on Windows — the template's PR-comment step contains emoji, and Python's open() defaults to the platform locale codepage (cp1252 on Windows), which cannot decode them and raises UnicodeDecodeError on a read that has nothing to do with the YAML itself being invalid. This is the same class of bug fixed in install.py's console-output handling earlier in this pack's history — worth remembering generally, not just here.

correctness_cases.fixture: evals/fixtures/violating_migration.sql, committed in a scratch git repo
correctness_cases.command: python3 scripts/baseline_audit.py --repo <scratch-repo>
correctness_cases.expect: status=audited on first run (no prior cache); the 5 known findings show as 'existing' (baseline-establishing), NOT as 'new' — a first-ever run must never be reported as 5 confirmed regressions
correctness_cases.why_it_matters: Conflating 'first run ever' with 'N new violations just introduced' would make every fresh adoption of this skill look like an alarming regression burst, when it's really just discovering pre-existing state for the first time.

correctness_cases.fixture: same repo as C20, run again immediately with no changes
correctness_cases.command: python3 scripts/baseline_audit.py --repo <scratch-repo>  (run twice in a row)
correctness_cases.expect: second run reports status=cached, does NOT re-invoke validate_schema.py
correctness_cases.why_it_matters: This is the entire point of the fingerprint cache — a session-start audit that re-scans the whole repo every single time defeats the 'keep startup fast' requirement from the brief.

correctness_cases.fixture: C20's repo, then a NEW commit adding evals/fixtures/destructive_migration.sql
correctness_cases.command: python3 scripts/baseline_audit.py --repo <scratch-repo>  (after the new commit)
correctness_cases.expect: status=audited (fingerprint changed via commit SHA), new=1 (the destructive-migration finding), existing=5 (unchanged from before), would_block=true
correctness_cases.why_it_matters: Confirms the fingerprint actually invalidates on a real commit, and that the NEW/EXISTING split correctly separates freshly-introduced findings from ones that were already known.

correctness_cases.fixture: C22's repo, then all violating files replaced with evals/fixtures/clean_migration.sql
correctness_cases.command: python3 scripts/baseline_audit.py --repo <scratch-repo>  (after replacing the violating files)
correctness_cases.expect: resolved=6 (all 6 prior findings across both files), new=0, existing=0
correctness_cases.why_it_matters: A cache that only tracks 'what's wrong now' without tracking 'what USED to be wrong and now isn't' can't answer 'did the fix work' — resolved-tracking is what makes that answerable without manually diffing two report files.

correctness_cases.fixture: an empty, non-git directory
correctness_cases.command: python3 scripts/baseline_audit.py --repo <empty-non-git-dir>
correctness_cases.why_it_matters: Must degrade gracefully (not crash, not hang) when pointed at something that isn't a git repo at all — a SessionStart hook that crashes the session over this would be worse than not having the audit.

correctness_cases.fixture: n/a
correctness_cases.command: python3 scripts/bypass_audit.py --check ""; --check "bypass"; --check "1"; --check "Fix Later"
correctness_cases.expect: all four rejected (exit 1), each with a specific, distinct explanation of why
correctness_cases.why_it_matters: Per the brief: 'Reject empty or generic values. Require a reason.' A bypass mechanism that accepts any truthy value provides zero actual accountability — it's exactly as auditable as no bypass tracking at all.

correctness_cases.fixture: a scratch git repo with a real commit, plus a validate_schema.py report.json for that repo
correctness_cases.command: python3 scripts/bypass_audit.py --record --repo <repo> --reason "INC-4821: ..." --actor "..." --findings-json report.json
correctness_cases.expect: exit 0, an audit record with the REAL git commit SHA (verified against `git rev-parse HEAD` in the same repo), the exact standards pulled from the findings file, appended to .data-standards-bypass-log.jsonl
correctness_cases.why_it_matters: The commit SHA and standard IDs must be the ACTUAL values from the real repo/findings, not placeholders — an audit record with fabricated or approximate values is worse than no record, since it creates false confidence that the bypass is traceable.

correctness_cases.fixture: same repo as C26, record a second, different bypass
correctness_cases.command: python3 scripts/bypass_audit.py --record --repo <repo> --reason "<different real reason>" --actor "<different actor>"  (run after C26 in the same repo)
correctness_cases.expect: .data-standards-bypass-log.jsonl has 2 lines, not 1 — the second record does not overwrite the first
correctness_cases.why_it_matters: An audit trail that only remembers the most recent bypass isn't an audit trail — every use must accumulate, since the whole point is answering 'how many times, and by whom, has this been bypassed.'

correctness_cases.fixture: same repo as C27
correctness_cases.command: python3 scripts/bypass_audit.py --record --repo <repo> --reason "bypass" --actor "someone"
correctness_cases.expect: exit 1, REJECTED message on stderr, the log file's line count is UNCHANGED (the bad attempt is not appended)
correctness_cases.why_it_matters: --record must apply the same validation as --check before writing anything — a script that validates only when explicitly asked to, but writes unconditionally on --record, would make the validation decorative.

correctness_cases.fixture: n/a
correctness_cases.command: python3 scripts/notify.py slack --event validation_failure --repo x --branch main --result FAIL  (no --channel, no env var set)
correctness_cases.expect: JSON result {"sent": false, "reason": "no channel configured..."}
correctness_cases.why_it_matters: Per the brief: notification failure must stay separate from — and never block — the standards result. A missing destination is the most common real-world case (most machines won't have this configured) and must degrade to a clear non-fatal report, not a crash.

correctness_cases.fixture: n/a (no SLACK_BOT_TOKEN in this environment's .env)
correctness_cases.command: python3 scripts/notify.py slack --event bypass --channel C0123456 --repo x --branch main --result FAIL
correctness_cases.expect: JSON result {"sent": false, "reason": "Slack token unavailable: ..."}
correctness_cases.why_it_matters: CAUGHT A REAL BUG: storytime/scripts/slack_send.py's load_token() raises SystemExit (not a catchable Exception) when SLACK_BOT_TOKEN is missing. notify.py's first draft only caught `except Exception`, so this case crashed with exit 1 — a direct violation of the brief's 'never block on notification unavailability' requirement. Fixed by adding an explicit `except SystemExit` clause. This eval case exists specifically to keep that fix from silently regressing.

correctness_cases.fixture: n/a
correctness_cases.command: call notify.sanitize() directly on strings containing C:\Users\..., /Users/.../..., /home/.../..., xoxb-..., sk-..., ghp_..., github_pat_...
correctness_cases.expect: every local-path pattern replaced with [local-path-redacted]; every credential pattern replaced with [credential-redacted]
correctness_cases.why_it_matters: Per the brief: never include credentials, absolute local paths, or full prompts in a Slack message or governance event. This is defense-in-depth (the fields this script accepts are structured, not free-text prompt dumps) but must actually work if a caller passes something it shouldn't.

correctness_cases.fixture: n/a
correctness_cases.command: call notify.sanitize_deep() on a dict containing a list with a mix of clean strings and a local path, plus a nested dict with a credential
correctness_cases.expect: every string value in every nesting level is sanitized; structure (dict/list shape) is preserved
correctness_cases.why_it_matters: The governance event has nested lists (changed_objects, issue_ids) and the Slack fields dict is itself nested — sanitization that only works on top-level strings would miss exactly the fields most likely to carry a stray local path or credential.

correctness_cases.fixture: n/a
correctness_cases.command: call build_governance_event() twice with IDENTICAL --repo/--head-sha/--result
correctness_cases.expect: the idempotency_key field is byte-identical across both calls
correctness_cases.why_it_matters: Per the brief: 'use ... idempotency keys' so a retried delivery doesn't double-count on the receiving side. A non-deterministic key (e.g. one including a timestamp) would defeat the entire point of idempotency.

correctness_cases.fixture: a scratch directory, no TALEEMABAD_GOVERNANCE_ENDPOINT set, no --endpoint passed
correctness_cases.command: python3 scripts/notify.py governance --repo x --branch main --head-sha abc --result PASS
correctness_cases.expect: delivery.sent=false with a reason naming the fallback file; .data-standards-governance-events.jsonl is created and contains the full event JSON on one line
correctness_cases.why_it_matters: Per the brief, 'full context' must never be silently discarded just because delivery isn't configured — a locally-preserved event can be forwarded later; a discarded one is gone.

correctness_cases.fixture: n/a
correctness_cases.command: python3 scripts/notify.py governance --endpoint https://this-domain-does-not-exist-12345.invalid/ingest --repo x --branch main --head-sha abc --result FAIL
correctness_cases.expect: delivery.sent=false, reason mentions 'all 3 attempts failed'; completes in well under a minute (bounded exponential backoff, not a hang)
correctness_cases.why_it_matters: Verified against a REAL DNS failure (an actually-nonexistent domain), not a mock — confirms the retry loop terminates, backs off, and reports clearly instead of hanging indefinitely or crashing the calling process on a real network failure.

correctness_cases.fixture: evals/fixtures/clean_migration.sql, staged in a scratch git repo, no bypass variable set
correctness_cases.command: a real `git commit` with the clean fixture staged
correctness_cases.why_it_matters: The bypass-gate rewrite must not regress the already-tested compliant-commit path — re-asserted here after the rewrite, not assumed unaffected.

correctness_cases.fixture: evals/fixtures/violating_migration.sql, staged, no bypass variable of either kind set
correctness_cases.command: a real `git commit` with the violating fixture staged
correctness_cases.why_it_matters: The default (no bypass attempted at all) path must still block exactly as before the rewrite — re-asserted, not assumed.

correctness_cases.fixture: evals/fixtures/violating_migration.sql, staged, TALEEMABAD_DATA_STANDARDS_BYPASS="bypass" (a rejected generic value)
correctness_cases.command: a real `git commit` with the violating fixture staged and the bypass var set to a rejected reason
correctness_cases.expect: stderr shows 'bypass REJECTED'; .data-standards-bypass-log.jsonl is NOT created (or, if it already existed, its line count is unchanged)
correctness_cases.why_it_matters: A rejected reason must behave EXACTLY as if no bypass had been attempted — falling through to the normal block, and critically, writing NO audit record. Recording a rejected bypass attempt as if it succeeded would be worse than not validating at all.

correctness_cases.fixture: evals/fixtures/violating_migration.sql, staged in a scratch repo WITH real commit history, TALEEMABAD_DATA_STANDARDS_BYPASS set to a real, specific reason
correctness_cases.command: a real `git commit` with the violating fixture staged and a valid bypass reason set
correctness_cases.expect: stderr shows 'BYPASSED'; .data-standards-bypass-log.jsonl gets a new line whose commit_sha EXACTLY matches a freshly-run `git rev-parse HEAD` in the same repo, and whose bypassed_finding_standards lists the real standards the violating fixture trips (D1, D3, D4, D5, D8)
correctness_cases.why_it_matters: The core guarantee of controlled bypass: a real, auditable trail with the REAL commit SHA and REAL bypassed standards, not placeholders. Verified in a repo with actual commit history (a repo with zero commits has no HEAD to record, which is a separate, correctly-handled case — see bypass_audit.py's own C26).

correctness_cases.fixture: evals/fixtures/violating_migration.sql, staged, CLAUDE_DATA_STANDARDS_GATE_OFF=1 set, no TALEEMABAD_DATA_STANDARDS_BYPASS
correctness_cases.command: a real `git commit` with the violating fixture staged and only the old-style variable set
correctness_cases.expect: stderr contains a NOTICE line naming the retired variable and pointing at the replacement, AND the commit is still blocked
correctness_cases.why_it_matters: Someone who still has the old variable set from muscle memory must be told clearly why nothing happened, rather than silently either bypassing (a security regression) or blocking with no explanation of why the thing that used to work no longer does.

correctness_cases.fixture: n/a (real .env in this pack, with TALEEMABAD_DATA_STANDARDS_SLACK_CHANNEL and SLACK_BOT_TOKEN configured; the invoking shell itself has neither exported)
correctness_cases.command: python3 scripts/notify.py slack --event validation_failure --repo x --branch main --commit abc --actor tester --result FAIL  (no --channel passed, TALEEMABAD_DATA_STANDARDS_SLACK_CHANNEL NOT exported in the calling shell)
correctness_cases.expect: JSON result {"sent": true, "ts": "<real timestamp>", "channel": "<the real channel ID from .env>"}
correctness_cases.why_it_matters: CAUGHT A REAL BUG during the gate-hook wiring: argparse's `--channel` default was `os.environ.get('TALEEMABAD_DATA_STANDARDS_SLACK_CHANNEL')`, evaluated at parse time — before slack_send's `_load_env()` (which reads the pack's own .env) ever ran, since that only happened later, deep inside send_slack(). A caller who configured the channel ONLY in the pack's .env (the whole point of 'configure once, works from any repo') got a false 'no channel configured' every time. Fixed by calling slack_send._load_env() at the very top of notify.py's main(), before argparse defaults are computed. Verified against the real, live-configured .env and a real chat.postMessage call that returned a genuine Slack ts — not a mock.

correctness_cases.fixture: evals/fixtures/violating_migration.sql, staged in a scratch git repo, real Slack credentials configured in the pack's .env, no bypass set
correctness_cases.command: a real `git commit` with the violating fixture staged
correctness_cases.expect: the commit is blocked exactly as before (stdout/stderr unchanged in content and timing), AND a real Slack message posts to the configured channel with event=validation_failure (verified by running the hook's exact notify_slack invocation synchronously and checking the returned ts, since the hook itself backgrounds the call and does not wait for or print its result)
correctness_cases.why_it_matters: This is the feature the user explicitly asked for: 'integrate notify.py in hooks so it works automatically.' The block behavior (exit 2, full findings on stderr) must be byte-for-byte the same as before Slack was wired in — the notification is a side effect layered on top, never a change to the gate's core contract.

correctness_cases.fixture: evals/fixtures/violating_migration.sql, staged, TALEEMABAD_DATA_STANDARDS_BYPASS set to a real valid reason, real Slack credentials configured
correctness_cases.command: a real `git commit` with the violating fixture staged and a valid bypass reason set
correctness_cases.expect: bypass recorded exactly as in C39 (unchanged), AND a real Slack message posts with event=bypass, actor, and the reason (verified the same way as C42 — by running the hook's exact notify_slack call synchronously)
correctness_cases.why_it_matters: A bypass is exactly the kind of event the Data Team needs to know about in real time, not just find later in a JSONL log nobody is watching — this closes that gap without changing the bypass mechanism's own exit-0/record behavior.

correctness_cases.fixture: evals/fixtures/violating_migration.sql, staged, TALEEMABAD_DATA_STANDARDS_SLACK_CHANNEL overridden in the calling shell to a nonexistent channel ID (simulating a broken Slack config)
correctness_cases.command: a real `git commit` with the violating fixture staged and a deliberately-broken Slack channel override exported
correctness_cases.expect: identical exit code and stderr content to C37 (no Slack involved at all) — the broken Slack config has zero observable effect on the gate's decision or output
correctness_cases.why_it_matters: This is the hook wiring's core safety constraint, confirmed by the user before implementation: 'a Slack-send failure must NEVER affect whether the commit is blocked.' The hook backgrounds the notify_slack call and never inspects its exit code or output, so even a hard Slack failure (bad channel, network down, missing token) cannot alter exit 0 vs exit 2 either way.

correctness_cases.fixture: evals/fixtures/violating_migration.sql, staged in a scratch git repo with `git config user.email` set to a real address, TALEEMABAD_USER_EMAIL NOT exported, a valid TALEEMABAD_DATA_STANDARDS_BYPASS reason set
correctness_cases.command: a real `git commit` with the violating fixture staged and a valid bypass reason set, in a repo where only git's own identity is configured
correctness_cases.expect: stderr's 'actor:' line and .data-standards-bypass-log.jsonl's actor field both show the real `git config user.email` value — NOT the OS username
correctness_cases.why_it_matters: CAUGHT A REAL GAP (2026-08-20, reported by the user asking 'is it capturing the user's email'): the actor fallback chain previously went straight from the unset TALEEMABAD_USER_EMAIL env var to the OS login name, even though `git config user.email` — the actual identity already required to make any commit at all — was sitting right there unused. Verified against a real scratch repo with a real configured git email and no TALEEMABAD_USER_EMAIL set: the bypass log and the Slack actor field both showed the real email, not a bare OS username.

correctness_cases.fixture: a scratch git repo with NO `git config user.email` set at all, TALEEMABAD_USER_EMAIL not exported
correctness_cases.command: resolve the same actor-fallback chain the gate hook uses, in a repo with no git identity configured
correctness_cases.expect: falls through cleanly to the OS username (no crash, no empty/blank actor field)
correctness_cases.why_it_matters: A repo with no git identity configured yet is a real, if less common, case (a fresh clone before anyone has run `git config user.email`) — the fallback chain must still degrade gracefully to something non-empty rather than erroring out or sending a blank actor field to Slack/the audit log.

correctness_cases.fixture: a scratch git repo with a nested subdirectory
correctness_cases.command: compare `basename "$(pwd)"` against the hook's actual REPO_NAME resolution (`git rev-parse --show-toplevel`'s basename) when invoked from the nested subdirectory, not the repo root
correctness_cases.expect: REPO_NAME correctly reports the repo's own top-level directory name (e.g. "my-repo"), not the subdirectory's name (e.g. "subdir") that a bare `basename "$(pwd)"` would have reported
correctness_cases.why_it_matters: The hook can fire from any point inside a repo, not just its root — `basename "$(pwd)"` alone would misreport the repo as whatever subdirectory the commit happened to be run from, which is exactly the kind of subtly-wrong attribution that erodes trust in the audit trail and Slack notifications over time.

orientation_cases.method: manual review: compare reference/orientation.md's "What the skill actually does" and "How to trigger it" sections against SKILL.md's inline orientation instructions
